newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: PNG says adventure is over for mercenaries.
newsitem.headline: PNG says adventure is over for mercenaries.

text.p: Mercenaries hired by the Papua New Guinea government to help put down a rebellion on Bougainville island would have been frontline fighters, not just mere consultants, according to their contract.

The 10-page legal contract was released hours before the mercenaries were escorted out of the South Pacific country on Friday, leaving it in turmoil but with millions of dollars in their bank accounts.

Major Walter Enuma, the soldier in charge of "Operation Rausim Kwik" (pidgin English for "remove them quickly"), oversaw the expulsion of the 61 mercenaries who were put on board a chartered Air New Guinea flight bound for Hong Kong.
"They wanted to go home, as far as they are concerned the adventure is over for them," Enuma told reporters.
The mercenaries, including their leader, retired British colonel Tim Spicer, were greeted at the airport by an onlooker who held up a banner saying "Tim Spicer you murderer get out of my country".

The "strictly confidential" contract between Papua New Guinea and British-based mercenary firm Sandline International was handed to journalists by the sacked army commander who sparked the country's crisis.

It showed that the South African veterans led by Spicer were not hired just to train troops but to conduct "offensive operations" to quell the Bougainville uprising and recapture a vast copper mine on the island.
Their US$36 million operation was thwarted by Brigadier-General Jerry Singirok, the army commander sacked after turning against Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan on Monday.
Singirok has been holed up inside Port Moresby's main Murray barracks throughout the crisis, briefing reporters in his backyard overlooking the Pacific ocean.
The contract was signed by Deputy Prime Minister Chris Haiveta and Spicer.

It stipulates that the mercenaries, described as "special constables", would "conduct offensive operations in Bougainville in conjunction with PNG defence forces to render the (Bougainville Revolutionary Army) militarily ineffective and repossess the Panguna mine".
Internationally condemned for hiring the mercenaries, Chan had said they would only be used to train PNG troops and would go to Bougainville only as consultants.
The contract states the mercenaries would be employed for an initial period of three months or until the BRA were defeated.
Fifty percent of the fee was to be paid when the contract was signed on January 31, with the remaining $18 million to be paid within 30 days of deployment.
An appendix at the back of the contract breaks down costs into $29 million for equipment and $7 million for manpower.
A 45-strong "special forces team" was costed at $4.5 million -- or $100,000 per soldier. PNG soldiers earn around $40 a week.
The nine-year secessionist rebellion on Bougainville began when landowners demanding compensation for mine works began attacking buses carrying miners.
The Panguna mine, one of the three largest in the world, was shut down in 1989. It is controlled by the Anglo-Australian company RTZ-CRA, the world's biggest mining group.

Thwarted by the soldiers they were meant to serve, the mercenaries never reached Bougainville. Spicer -- who signed his contract "Tim Spicer OBE", or Order of the British Empire -- and his mostly South African soldiers of fortune never had a chance to fulfill their contract.
